idiom_name: class with a #private array, Iterable<Order> and readonly Order[] exposure
implementation_notes: TypeScript replaces the unmodifiable-wrapper machinery with the type system: return `readonly Order[]` (ReadonlyArray<Order>) and the compiler removes every mutating method and index assignment from the caller's view at zero runtime cost. The owner side is a class with a #private array (runtime privacy, so the container cannot be reached even from JavaScript) plus an add method that enforces the invariants; implementing Iterable<Order> keeps for...of, spread and destructuring working. Because readonly is erased at runtime, a JavaScript caller or a cast can still mutate a returned array - return a copy for values that leave the process, and treat ReadonlyArray as a contract with TypeScript callers rather than a runtime barrier.
pitfalls: readonly/ReadonlyArray exist only in the type system: a JavaScript caller or an `as` cast can still push into the returned array, so copy defensively where that matters.
Structural typing accepts any object with the same members; a class with a private or #private field is compared nominally, which is the only way to brand the domain type.
`readonly items: Order[]` blocks reassigning the property but not items.push(...); use ReadonlyArray<Order> for an element-level guarantee.
#private fields are invisible to serialization (JSON.stringify yields {}) and are not inherited by subclasses - provide toJSON() or project to a DTO at the wire boundary.
